questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain why identity must be square
questions.stem: Why must an identity matrix be square?

answer.exemplar: An identity needs equal rows and columns so that for any compatible matrix A, both AI and IA are defined and both return A, which requires matching A's dimensions on both sides.

questions.explanation: For I to serve as identity for multiplication on both sides, its dimensions must match A's columns (right) and rows (left), forcing squareness.
questions.hint: Both sides require matching dimensions.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: Explain zero product with nonzero factors
questions.stem: Explain how two nonzero matrices can multiply to zero in the astronomer's log.

answer.exemplar: The columns of the right factor can lie in the null space of the left factor, so each product entry is a dot product that cancels to zero without either matrix being zero.

questions.explanation: When B's columns are in A's null space, A maps them to zero, giving AB=0 with both factors nonzero.
questions.hint: Null space of left factor contains right factor's columns.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: Summarize why order matters
questions.stem: Summarize why an astronomer checks the order of factors before computing a matrix product.

answer.exemplar: Order affects both whether the product exists, since inner dimensions must match, and its value, since matrix multiplication is not commutative even when both orders are defined.

questions.explanation: Order determines dimension compatibility and, when both orders exist, the resulting matrix can differ.
questions.hint: Compatibility and value both depend on order.
